title: The Relief of Coming Clean
overview: A poet describes how hiding a wrong left him sick and drained, and how admitting it to God brought forgiveness, safety and joy.

parts.label: The happiness of forgiveness (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The poem uses three pictures for forgiveness: a wrong lifted away (one sense of the Hebrew word), a shameful thing covered over, and a debt God no longer counts against someone. The happy person here is not sinless but honest with God, hiding nothing and not fooling themselves.

parts.label: The cost of staying silent (vv. 3-4)
parts.note: While the writer refused to admit his wrong, guilt wore him down in body and mind, and his strength drained away as if in the dry heat of summer. He felt this as God's hand pressing on him day and night.

parts.label: Confession and quick release (v. 5)
parts.note: Once he stopped covering up and said he would confess, the poem says God forgave the guilt of his sin. The silence brought only misery, while the decision to speak brought release.

parts.label: An invitation to others (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: Because of what happened to him, he urges faithful people to pray while God may be found, using rising floodwaters as a picture of overwhelming danger that will not reach them. He calls God his hiding place, who protects him from trouble and surrounds him with songs of rescue.

parts.label: Teaching, not a bridle (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: A voice promises to guide the reader with a caring, watchful eye, though it is unclear whether God or the writer is speaking. Unlike a horse or mule that must be steered with a metal bit, people are invited to come willingly, and the poem ends with a call to rejoice in the LORD's unfailing love.

think: What does keeping something hidden cost a person, and what changes when it is finally said out loud?
